claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a simple single-phase solid solution at room temperature.
Single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness.
Single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low yield strength.
The low hardness and strength are governed by an inability of CoCrFeNiTi to develop significant short-range chemical order or nanoscale precipitates.
Short-range chemical order and nanoscale precipitates can act as effective obstacles to dislocation glide.
In the absence of short-range order and nanoscale precipitates, dislocation motion in CoCrFeNiTi is relatively uninhibited.
Relatively uninhibited dislocation motion produces high plasticity in CoCrFeNiTi.
Relatively uninhibited dislocation motion gives CoCrFeNiTi favorable machinability.
The lattice distortions in simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi are insufficient to impede dislocation glide.
Promoting short-range order or precipitation increases localized lattice distortion.
The localized distortions or precipitates impede dislocation movement.
Promoting short-range order or nanoscale precipitation will increase the yield strength of CoCrFeNiTi relative to the baseline.
Promoting short-range order or nanoscale precipitation will increase the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi relative to the baseline.
The increase in strength and hardness will be accompanied by reduced ductility.
A controlled heat treatment can stimulate short-range order or nanoscale precipitation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Minor alloying additions can stimulate short-range order or nanoscale precipitation without altering the overall composition.
The proposed mechanism applies under quasi-static loading from room temperature to approximately 600 °C.
As-cast or conventionally processed equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has a homogeneous solid-solution structure.

contradictions.description: The proposal invokes minor alloying or compositional adjustments while also requiring that the overall composition not be altered; adding or adjusting alloying elements necessarily changes composition unless a specific compensating substitution is defined.

The boundary restricts the hypothesis to alloys maintained as single-phase solid solutions, whereas the intervention is intended to form nanoscale precipitates, which would make the modified material no longer strictly single phase.

The mechanism says ductility may possibly decrease, the predicted outcome states that ductility will decrease, and the falsification rule treats unchanged ductility as falsifying the hypothesis. Unchanged ductility would not falsify the central proposed link between added obstacles and increased hardness or strength.
